I fully support it, provided it's not a technical skill.

In my view, there's a huge difference between someone falsifying a technical skill (say, machining for example) and something more trivial such as management or supervisory experience. My experience has been that companies are often extremely reluctant to promote people to management or supervisory positions, even if talent is staring them right in the face, and will instead choose to hire people who have either graduated directly into management or lucked out or brown nosed their way into it. In many cases these managers and supervisors lack management ability and people skills in general, causing decreased productivity and resignations.

Also I've come across so many job listings that have utterly ridiculous entry requirements. Anyone who actually had the requisite qualifications would be massively underemployed in such a position, which forces me to conclude that the employer believes that qualifications and previous experience are a substitute for structuring an interview to screen for aptitude. Or to put it another way; the employer is being lazy.

To expand further on the qualifications bit, there are many people out there who are obscenely intelligent and very well educated, but have no formal education to speak of. These people may have been at a social disadvantage due to not having the money or the means to attend school, and are likely to see it as a rather arbitrary barrier to convey what might've been better established if that person was to have simply been given a work trial.

One other thing to note, is that frequently employers will promote and hire in a way that is completely unfair and even puts whole groups at a disadvantage. Everything from hiring based on race, to looks, to who your friends are or what accent you have.

So in summary, I feel that "fluffing up" a resume levels the playing field somewhat, and acts to combat what are arguably unethical recruitment practices and inequalities. However I do feel that there are obvious practical limitations such as technical skills that would be difficult if not impossible to avoid without formal education.
